path.name: Your First Digital Product
path.tagline: Make one small digital product that solves a real problem and put it in front of buyers.
path.description: You pick one problem your audience will pay to solve, check that people already look for help with it, and build a small first version with free tools. Over 30 days you put it on a simple sales page, set an honest beginner price, start a small email list and share helpful content that points to it. Sales usually start slowly, so the goal is a launched product, real feedback and at least one genuine first sale attempt.
path.objective: Validate one problem, create a small version 1 of a digital product, publish its sales page, make a first sale attempt by Day 14 and finish with real numbers and a plan for the next 30 days.
path.typicalPrice: Small products usually sell for $5–$30 to start
firstTasks: Write down who you help and the one problem your product will solve
Collect 15 real questions your audience asks online
Outline a small product you can finish in about a week
Publish your sales page and make your first sale attempt by Day 14
workflow: Pick one specific problem your audience already asks about
Check what already sells for that problem and at what price
Outline a small product that solves one part of it well
Build version 1 with free tools and only licensed fonts and images
Put it on one selling platform with a clear sales page and fair price
Share helpful content and emails that point to the product
Read your visits and sales, ask buyers for feedback, then improve

weeks.title: Build & List
focus: Sales page and first sale attempt

tools.name: Canva
tools.purpose: Design printables, templates, covers and preview images

tools.name: Google Docs
tools.purpose: Write guides and ebooks, then export them as PDF

tools.name: Google Slides
tools.purpose: Lay out workbooks and slides for a mini-course

tools.name: Notion
tools.purpose: Build and share Notion templates and keep your plan in one place

tools.name: Google Forms
tools.purpose: Run a short survey and collect buyer feedback

tools.name: Selling platform
tools.purpose: Pick one, such as Gumroad, Etsy, Payhip, Stan or Ko-fi, to host your product page
tools.cost: Free to start, fees per sale

plan.missionTitle: Decide who you help and which problem your product will solve.
plan.goal: Write a one-sentence product promise and your 30-day goal.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 1 lesson
tasks.description: See how small digital products work: one audience, one painful problem, one simple fix people can download today.

tasks.title: Name your audience
tasks.description: Write who you want to help in plain words. Be specific enough that one person could read it and think "that is me".

tasks.title: List five problems
tasks.description: Write five problems that audience has that a guide, template, checklist or printable could help with.

tasks.title: Write your product promise
tasks.description: Use this shape: "I help [audience] [get result] without [frustration]." Keep it to one sentence.

tasks.title: Set your 30-day goal
tasks.description: Choose a goal you control, such as "publish my sales page and make one sale attempt". Sales numbers are not fully in your control yet.

plan.nicheHint: Start from this draft: I help {audience} with {problem}. Then circle the one problem in your list that {audience} would most want solved this week.

stageHints.idea: Pick the audience you understand best, ideally one you belong to or used to belong to.
stageHints.started: Look at what you already made and write the promise it was really trying to keep.
stageHints.some_traction: Write the promise around the problem your first buyers bought for, not the one you guessed.
stageHints.already_earning: Write down which product sells most and the problem it solves; this month builds on that.

plan.missionTitle: Find the exact words your audience uses when they ask for help.
plan.goal: Collect 15 real questions about your problem.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 2 lesson
tasks.description: Learn where buyers describe their problems in public and how to read those places without joining the noise.

tasks.title: Search Reddit and forums
tasks.description: Search your topic plus words like "help", "how do I" or "struggling". Copy questions word for word.

tasks.title: Read Pinterest and YouTube comments
tasks.description: Open popular pins and videos on your topic and note questions people ask in the comments.

tasks.title: Group the questions
tasks.description: Sort your 15 questions into three or four groups. The biggest group is your strongest signal.

plan.nicheHint: Search for {terms} and note how {audience} describe {problem} in their own words. Their phrasing will become your product title later.

stageHints.idea: Collect questions with an open mind; your first idea may change, and that is fine.
stageHints.started: Check whether the questions match what you already made, and note any gaps.
stageHints.some_traction: Look for questions your buyers asked you directly; they are the most valuable.
stageHints.already_earning: Look for new questions near your best seller; they may point to your next product.

plan.missionTitle: See what already sells for your problem and at what price.
plan.goal: Fill in a list of 10 similar products with their format and price.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 3 lesson
tasks.description: Competition is a good sign: it shows people already pay for help with this problem. Learn what to look for.

tasks.title: Search one or two marketplaces
tasks.description: Search your topic on marketplaces such as Etsy or Gumroad's Discover page. Note 10 products that solve a similar problem.

tasks.title: Record format and price
tasks.description: For each product write the format, the price and roughly how many reviews it has.

tasks.title: Read the reviews
tasks.description: Read the 2 and 3 star reviews. Write down what buyers wished was included or done better.

tasks.title: Find your angle
tasks.description: Write one sentence on how your version could be clearer, more specific or easier to use. Never copy another product.

plan.nicheHint: Search for {terms} on one marketplace and note what similar products for {audience} cost. Look for a gap, such as a narrower audience or a simpler format.

stageHints.idea: Treat this as research only; you are learning the market, not choosing a winner yet.
stageHints.started: Compare your existing product with the top three and note one clear difference.
stageHints.some_traction: Check whether your price sits far above or below similar products, and note why.
stageHints.already_earning: Look for problems close to your best seller that nobody serves well yet.

plan.missionTitle: Ask real people which version of your idea they want most.
plan.goal: Get at least five answers to a short survey or poll.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 4 lesson
tasks.description: A short survey turns guesses into evidence. Learn how to ask questions that get honest answers.

tasks.title: Write three questions
tasks.description: Ask what they struggle with, what they have tried and what would help most. Keep it under two minutes.

tasks.title: Build it in Google Forms
tasks.description: Make a free form, or use a poll feature on a platform where you already have followers.

tasks.title: Share it respectfully
tasks.description: Send it to friends who fit your audience, or post it where surveys are allowed. Read each group's rules first.

tasks.title: Note the patterns
tasks.description: After a day or two, write the top two answers in your worksheet.

plan.nicheHint: Ask {audience} which part of {problem} takes the most time or causes the most stress. Their top answer is a strong candidate for your product.

stageHints.idea: Five honest answers are enough to start; you are looking for patterns, not proof.
stageHints.started: Ask people who saw your earlier attempt what would have made it worth paying for.
stageHints.some_traction: Survey your buyers or followers about the next problem they want solved.
stageHints.already_earning: Ask your customers what they would buy next and at what price would feel fair.

plan.missionTitle: Choose one small product format that fits your time and skills.
plan.goal: Choose a format and a working title.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 5 lesson
tasks.description: Compare common beginner formats, such as printables, templates, short guides and preset packs, by effort and fit.

tasks.title: List three formats
tasks.description: Write three formats that could solve your problem, such as a checklist, a Notion or Canva template, a printable planner or a short guide.

tasks.title: Score them
tasks.description: Score each from 1 to 5 on time to make, fit with your skills and how quickly it helps the buyer.

tasks.title: Pick one
tasks.description: Choose the highest score. Small and finished beats big and unfinished.

tasks.title: Write a working title
tasks.description: Name the result, not the format, for example "The 15-Minute Weekly Budget Template".

plan.nicheHint: Pick the format that solves {problem} fastest for {audience}. A one-page tool they can use today often beats a long ebook.

stageHints.idea: Choose something you could finish in five working sessions.
stageHints.started: If your first product was too big, choose a smaller format that solves one part of it.
stageHints.some_traction: Pick a format your buyers already said they like using.
stageHints.already_earning: Choose a format that pairs with your best seller so it can become a bundle later.

plan.missionTitle: Turn your idea into a clear outline before you design anything.
plan.goal: Finish a one-page outline of your product.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 6 lesson
tasks.description: Learn to outline backwards from the result: start with what the buyer can do at the end, then list the steps.

tasks.title: Write the end result
tasks.description: Describe what the buyer will have or be able to do after using your product.

tasks.title: List the sections
tasks.description: Write five to eight sections or pages that get them there, in order.

tasks.title: Cut ruthlessly
tasks.description: Remove anything that is nice to know but not needed for the result.

tasks.title: Note what is included
tasks.description: Write a plain list of files, pages and formats the buyer will get. You will reuse it on your sales page.

plan.nicheHint: Outline the steps {audience} need to go from stuck to done with {problem}. Use the questions you collected as section headings.

stageHints.idea: Keep version 1 small; you can always add a second edition later.
stageHints.started: Outline the existing product again and mark what to cut, fix or finish.
stageHints.some_traction: Rebuild the outline around what buyers said they used most.
stageHints.already_earning: Outline a companion product that starts where your best seller ends.

plan.missionTitle: Learn what you can legally use and collect your fonts and images.
plan.goal: Finish the licensing checklist and gather your assets.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 7 lesson
tasks.description: Fonts, images and templates all come with licenses. Learn the basics so your product is safe to sell.

tasks.title: Go through the checklist
tasks.description: Read each item and tick what applies to your product.

tasks.title: Collect licensed assets
tasks.description: Use your own photos or fonts and images whose license allows commercial use in products for sale. Save the license notes.

tasks.title: Skip PLR and copies
tasks.description: Do not resell other people's material or bought PLR content as your own work. Write everything in your own words.

tasks.title: Review your week
tasks.description: Look at your outline, survey answers and price notes. Write one sentence on what you learned this week.

plan.nicheHint: If your topic for {audience} touches health, money or legal questions, plan an educational framing and a clear disclaimer now so it is built in from the start.

stageHints.idea: Starting clean is easy: use your own words and properly licensed assets from day one.
stageHints.started: Check the fonts and images in what you already made and replace anything you cannot confirm.
stageHints.some_traction: Audit your listed product for licensing before more people buy it.
stageHints.already_earning: Do a full licensing check across your products and keep the notes in one folder.

plan.missionTitle: Create the core content of your product.
plan.goal: Finish the first full draft of the content.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 8 lesson
tasks.description: Version 1 is about finished, not perfect. Learn how to draft fast with free tools and fix things later.

tasks.title: Set up your file
tasks.description: Open Canva, Google Docs, Slides or Notion, whichever fits your format, and paste your outline in.

tasks.title: Draft every section
tasks.description: Fill each section with plain, direct steps. Use short sentences and examples.

tasks.title: Mark gaps, keep moving
tasks.description: When you get stuck, write [fix later] and move on to the next section.

tasks.title: Time-box it
tasks.description: Stop when your session ends, even if it is rough. You will polish tomorrow.

plan.nicheHint: Write each section as if you are helping one person from {audience} with {problem} right next to you. Plain words beat clever ones.

stageHints.idea: Aim for a complete rough draft, not a beautiful one.
stageHints.started: Reuse what you already made and fill only the gaps your outline shows.
stageHints.some_traction: Fix the parts buyers struggled with first, then draft anything new.
stageHints.already_earning: Draft the companion product using the same structure as your best seller.

plan.missionTitle: Make your product look clean and export the final files.
plan.goal: Have a finished version 1 file ready to deliver.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 9 lesson
tasks.description: Simple design rules that make any product feel trustworthy: one or two fonts, plenty of space and clear headings.

tasks.title: Apply a simple style
tasks.description: Choose one heading font, one body font and two colors. Only use fonts and images you are licensed to use.

tasks.title: Fill the [fix later] gaps
tasks.description: Go back through the draft and finish every marked gap.

tasks.title: Export and test
tasks.description: Export as PDF or share link. Open it on your phone and computer to check that it works and reads well.

tasks.title: Ask one person to try it
tasks.description: Send it to a friend who fits your audience and ask whether anything is confusing.

plan.nicheHint: Make sure someone from {audience} could open the file and start solving {problem} within five minutes. If not, add a short "start here" page.

stageHints.idea: Finishing this file is a big step; most people never get here.
stageHints.started: Give your existing product a clean refresh rather than starting over.
stageHints.some_traction: Polish what buyers see first: the cover, the start page and the first section.
stageHints.already_earning: Use the same style as your other products so they look like a set.

plan.missionTitle: Choose one selling platform and set up your shop.
plan.goal: Create your account and an empty product draft.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 10 lesson
tasks.description: Compare common platforms such as Gumroad, Etsy, Payhip, Stan and Ko-fi on fees, audience and setup time. Then pick one.

tasks.title: Compare two or three
tasks.description: Read each platform's current fees and rules for digital products. Write them in a short table.

tasks.title: Pick one
tasks.description: Choose the one that fits your format and audience. You can always add another later.

tasks.title: Set up your shop
tasks.description: Create your account, add your name, a short bio and a profile picture. Follow the platform's setup steps for payouts.

tasks.title: Start a product draft
tasks.description: Add a product draft with your working title. Leave it unpublished for now.

plan.nicheHint: Think about where {audience} already shop. If they browse marketplaces, a marketplace may help; if you will send them yourself, a simple storefront may be enough.

stageHints.idea: Pick the platform with the simplest setup; speed matters more than features right now.
stageHints.started: If your current platform works, keep it and focus on the product page instead.
stageHints.some_traction: Stay where your sales are happening and improve the page before switching.
stageHints.already_earning: Only add a second platform if your buyers clearly shop there.

plan.missionTitle: Choose a beginner price you can explain.
plan.goal: Write your price and the reason for it.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 11 lesson
tasks.description: Pricing is a starting point you can change. Learn a simple way to set a fair beginner price.

tasks.title: Look at your research
tasks.description: Use the prices you noted on Day 3 to find the usual range for similar products.

tasks.title: Fill the pricing worksheet
tasks.description: Consider the result it gives, how much time it saves and how complete it is.

tasks.title: Pick one number
tasks.description: Choose a price inside the range. Avoid pricing far below everyone else just because you are new.

tasks.title: Write your reasoning
tasks.description: Write one sentence on why this price is fair. You will revisit it after the first sales.

plan.nicheHint: Ask what solving {problem} is worth to {audience} in time or stress saved. Price for that, within the range similar products already sell for.

stageHints.idea: Pick a simple starting price inside the usual range and commit to it for now.
stageHints.started: If your old price got no sales, check the page and the traffic before cutting the price.
stageHints.some_traction: Consider a small price increase if buyers say it was easily worth it.
stageHints.already_earning: Test a slightly higher price on your next product rather than discounting the current one.

plan.missionTitle: Write a simple sales page that explains your product clearly.
plan.goal: Have a full sales page draft with preview images.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 12 lesson
tasks.description: A good sales page answers six questions: what it does, who it is for, what is inside, what it costs, what it looks like and what if.

tasks.title: Write the promise and who it is for
tasks.description: Use the sales page template for the headline, the short intro and a "this is for you if" list.

tasks.title: List what is included
tasks.description: Use your Day 6 list. Be clear about format, page count and what the buyer will not get.

tasks.title: Make three preview images
tasks.description: Create preview images in Canva that show real pages of the product, not just the cover.

tasks.title: Add a short FAQ
tasks.description: Answer three questions, such as how delivery works, what devices it works on and your refund policy.

plan.nicheHint: Use the exact words {audience} used for {problem} on Day 2 in your headline. People buy when they recognize their own situation.

stageHints.idea: Write it plainly; clear beats clever on a first sales page.
stageHints.started: Rewrite your existing page with the template and compare the two versions.
stageHints.some_traction: Add any buyer feedback you have and tighten the headline.
stageHints.already_earning: Reuse what works on your best seller's page and adapt it here.

plan.missionTitle: Publish your product page and test the full buying flow.
plan.goal: Your product is live and the purchase flow works.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 13 lesson
tasks.description: Before you share anything, test the full buying flow so your first buyer has a smooth experience.

tasks.title: Run the launch checklist
tasks.description: Check title, price, files, preview images, description and refund policy.

tasks.title: Publish the product
tasks.description: Switch the product from draft to live on your platform.

tasks.title: Test the flow
tasks.description: Use the platform's preview or test option, or buy it yourself if needed, to confirm the file arrives correctly.

tasks.title: Save your link
tasks.description: Save the product link somewhere you can copy it quickly. You will share it tomorrow.

plan.nicheHint: Read your live page as if you are someone from {audience} who has never heard of you. Is it clear within ten seconds how it helps with {problem}?

stageHints.idea: Pressing publish is the hardest part; a live page is worth more than a perfect draft.
stageHints.started: Relaunch your existing product with the new page and fresh preview images.
stageHints.some_traction: Publish the updated version and let past buyers know about the update.
stageHints.already_earning: Publish the new product and link to it from your best seller's page.

plan.missionTitle: Share your product with people who already know you.
plan.goal: Make your first sale attempt with at least five people.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 14 lesson
tasks.description: Your first sales usually come from people who already know or trust you. Learn how to share without being pushy.

tasks.title: List ten people
tasks.description: Write ten people or one small community who fit your audience or know someone who does.

tasks.title: Write a short honest message
tasks.description: Say what you made, who it is for, the price and that feedback is welcome. Keep it to a few lines.

tasks.title: Share it
tasks.description: Send it personally to people you know, or post once in a community where sharing your work is allowed. Follow its rules.

tasks.title: Note every response
tasks.description: Write down who replied, any questions and any purchases. Questions are useful even without a sale.

plan.nicheHint: Tell people you made something to help {audience} with {problem}. Ask them to pass it on to someone who fits, rather than asking them to buy.

stageHints.idea: A first sale attempt is a win even if nobody buys yet; you learn what people ask.
stageHints.started: Share the improved version with people who saw the first one and tell them what changed.
stageHints.some_traction: Thank your past buyers and ask whether they know someone who would find it useful.
stageHints.already_earning: Tell your existing customers about the new product with a short, honest message.

plan.missionTitle: Create a free resource that helps people and leads to your product.
plan.goal: Finish a small free lead magnet.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 15 lesson
tasks.description: A lead magnet is a small free resource that solves a tiny piece of the problem and lets people join your email list.

tasks.title: Pick an idea
tasks.description: Choose one idea from the lead magnet list that solves one small part of your problem.

tasks.title: Build it fast
tasks.description: Make it in one sitting with the same tools and style as your product.

tasks.title: Point to the product
tasks.description: Add a short final page that explains how your paid product helps with the rest of the problem.

tasks.title: Keep it genuinely useful
tasks.description: Make sure the freebie helps on its own. Nobody likes a free resource that is only an advert.

plan.nicheHint: Create a one-page freebie that solves the first small step of {problem} for {audience}, such as a checklist or quick-start sheet.

stageHints.idea: Keep it small; a single useful page is enough.
stageHints.started: Turn one section of your existing product into a free sample.
stageHints.some_traction: Make the freebie about the question new buyers ask most often.
stageHints.already_earning: Use a lead magnet to grow the list that will hear about all your products.

plan.missionTitle: Set up a free email signup and a short welcome email.
plan.goal: Your signup form works and sends a welcome email.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 16 lesson
tasks.description: Email lets you reach interested people directly. Learn how to set up a simple list for free.

tasks.title: Choose a free tool
tasks.description: Use your selling platform's built-in email feature if it has one, or the free plan of an email tool.

tasks.title: Create a signup form
tasks.description: Make a form that delivers your lead magnet. Only ask for a first name and email.

tasks.title: Write the welcome email
tasks.description: Use the welcome sequence script. Deliver the freebie, say who you are and what to expect.

tasks.title: Test it
tasks.description: Sign up with your own email to check the freebie arrives. Follow the tool's rules on consent and unsubscribe links.

plan.nicheHint: Write your welcome email to someone from {audience} who just downloaded help with {problem}. Tell them what kind of emails they will get.

stageHints.idea: A list of even a few people is a real start.
stageHints.started: Invite anyone who showed interest earlier to join, with their permission.
stageHints.some_traction: Ask past buyers if they want to join for updates and new resources.
stageHints.already_earning: Connect your list to every product page so new buyers can opt in.

plan.missionTitle: Plan helpful posts that point people to your product.
plan.goal: Have six post ideas planned for this week.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 17 lesson
tasks.description: Content that teaches something useful earns attention without ads. Learn how to link it to your product naturally.

tasks.title: Pick one or two channels
tasks.description: Choose where your audience spends time, such as Pinterest, short videos or a social platform you already use.

tasks.title: Write six post ideas
tasks.description: Use the launch post ideas list to plan six helpful posts that each solve a small problem.

tasks.title: Add a soft call to action
tasks.description: End each post with one line that points to your freebie or product.

tasks.title: Schedule your week
tasks.description: Put each post on a day in your calendar for the next week.

plan.nicheHint: Turn each of the Day 2 questions from {audience} into a post. Each one should help with a small part of {problem} on its own.

stageHints.idea: Start with one channel; spreading thin across five rarely works.
stageHints.started: Reuse the channel where you already have a few followers.
stageHints.some_traction: Plan posts around results your buyers told you about.
stageHints.already_earning: Plan content that introduces the new product to your current audience.

plan.missionTitle: Publish your first launch content and share your product.
plan.goal: Publish two posts that point to your product or freebie.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 18 lesson
tasks.description: Launch day is just the day you start sharing consistently. Learn how to make it calm and repeatable.

tasks.title: Publish two posts
tasks.description: Publish the first two posts from your plan, each with your link or freebie.

tasks.title: Update your profiles
tasks.description: Add your product or freebie link to your bio on the channels you use.

tasks.title: Reply to every comment
tasks.description: Answer questions quickly and helpfully. Do not argue or pressure anyone.

tasks.title: Write down what happened
tasks.description: Note views, clicks and any signups or sales. Small numbers are normal at this stage.

plan.nicheHint: Open your posts with the problem {audience} have, not with your product. Show one quick tip for {problem}, then mention what you made.

stageHints.idea: Publishing at all is the win today; reach grows with consistency.
stageHints.started: Publish posts that show what changed in the improved version.
stageHints.some_traction: Share a short buyer result, with permission, alongside a helpful tip.
stageHints.already_earning: Announce the new product to your audience and list on the same day.

plan.missionTitle: Create visual content that can keep bringing visitors.
plan.goal: Publish three pins or short videos.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 19 lesson
tasks.description: Pinterest pins and short videos can send visitors for a long time. Learn simple formats that work for digital products.

tasks.title: Make three visuals
tasks.description: In Canva, create three pins or record three short videos showing a real page or tip from your product.

tasks.title: Write searchable titles
tasks.description: Use the words your audience searches for in titles and descriptions.

tasks.title: Link correctly
tasks.description: Point each one to your product page or freebie signup.

tasks.title: Publish and note
tasks.description: Publish all three and write down where you posted them.

plan.nicheHint: Use {terms} in your titles and descriptions so {audience} can find your pins or videos when they search for help with {problem}.

stageHints.idea: Copy a simple format you like and make it your own.
stageHints.started: Make visuals from pages people already liked in your product.
stageHints.some_traction: Turn your most clicked post into a pin or short video.
stageHints.already_earning: Create a set of visuals for each product so they support each other.

plan.missionTitle: Help in one online community and share only where it is allowed.
plan.goal: Make three helpful replies in one community.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 20 lesson
tasks.description: Communities reward people who help first. Learn how to take part without spamming.

tasks.title: Read the rules
tasks.description: Pick one community where your audience gathers and read its rules about self-promotion.

tasks.title: Answer three questions
tasks.description: Give complete, helpful answers that do not need your product to be useful.

tasks.title: Share only if allowed
tasks.description: If the rules allow it, mention your product or freebie once where it is relevant. If not, link only from your profile.

tasks.title: Note the questions
tasks.description: Add any new questions you saw to your idea list.

plan.nicheHint: Answer questions from {audience} about {problem} fully. A genuinely helpful answer makes people curious about what else you have made.

stageHints.idea: Show up as a helper first; trust comes before sales.
stageHints.started: Join a community you have not tried yet and listen before posting.
stageHints.some_traction: Keep helping in the community where your buyers came from.
stageHints.already_earning: Help regularly in one community instead of posting once in many.

plan.missionTitle: Ask buyers and testers what worked and what did not.
plan.goal: Get feedback from at least three people.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 21 lesson
tasks.description: Feedback tells you what to fix and what to say on your sales page. Learn how to ask so people actually reply.

tasks.title: Pick who to ask
tasks.description: List your buyers, testers and anyone who downloaded the freebie.

tasks.title: Send the request
tasks.description: Use the feedback request script and ask two or three short questions.

tasks.title: Group the answers
tasks.description: Sort what you hear into "keep", "fix" and "add later".

tasks.title: Review your week
tasks.description: Write one sentence on what surprised you most this week.

plan.nicheHint: Ask {audience} which part of the product helped most with {problem} and where they got stuck.

stageHints.idea: If you have no buyers yet, ask your testers and freebie readers.
stageHints.started: Ask the people who looked but did not buy what held them back.
stageHints.some_traction: Ask buyers what result they got and whether you can quote them.
stageHints.already_earning: Ask your best customers what they would want next.

plan.missionTitle: Fix the most important issues buyers or testers found.
plan.goal: Publish version 1.1 of your product.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 22 lesson
tasks.description: Small improvements based on real feedback beat big redesigns. Learn how to choose what to fix first.

tasks.title: Pick the top three fixes
tasks.description: Choose the three "fix" items that would help the most people.

tasks.title: Make the changes
tasks.description: Update the file in the same tool you made it in.

tasks.title: Upload the new version
tasks.description: Replace the file on your platform and check the download works.

tasks.title: Tell past buyers
tasks.description: Let earlier buyers know there is an updated version they can download.

plan.nicheHint: Fix whatever stopped {audience} from making progress on {problem}. Clarity fixes usually matter more than design fixes.

stageHints.idea: If nobody has used it yet, improve the start page and the first section.
stageHints.started: Fix what testers found confusing, then reshare the improved version.
stageHints.some_traction: Fix what buyers mentioned more than once.
stageHints.already_earning: Apply the same fixes across your other products if they share the issue.

plan.missionTitle: Ask for testimonials and add social proof to your page.
plan.goal: Add at least one real testimonial or buyer note to your page.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 23 lesson
tasks.description: Real words from real buyers help new visitors trust you. Learn how to ask honestly and use them fairly.

tasks.title: Ask for permission
tasks.description: Ask happy buyers or testers if you can quote them, using the script.

tasks.title: Keep it real
tasks.description: Only use real words from real people, with permission. Never write or edit reviews to make them sound better.

tasks.title: Add them to your page
tasks.description: Place one or two short testimonials near the price or the FAQ.

tasks.title: Thank everyone
tasks.description: Thank each person who replied, whether or not they gave a quote.

plan.nicheHint: A short quote from someone in {audience} about how the product helped with {problem} is more convincing than anything you write yourself.

stageHints.idea: If you have no testimonials yet, add a short note on who tested it and what you changed.
stageHints.started: Ask your testers for a one-line quote about the improved version.
stageHints.some_traction: Pick the testimonial that names a specific result and put it near the top.
stageHints.already_earning: Collect testimonials into one file so you can reuse them across pages.

plan.missionTitle: Look at your visits, conversion rate and sales.
plan.goal: Write down your three key numbers.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 24 lesson
tasks.description: Three numbers tell you most of what you need: page visits, conversion rate and sales. Learn what each one means.

tasks.title: Find your page visits
tasks.description: Open your platform's analytics and note visits to your product page since launch.

tasks.title: Count your sales
tasks.description: Note how many sales you have. Zero is a real number and still useful.

tasks.title: Work out your conversion rate
tasks.description: Divide sales by visits. With few visits, treat it as a rough signal, not a verdict.

tasks.title: Name the bottleneck
tasks.description: If visits are low, the issue is traffic. If visits are fine but sales are low, look at the page and the offer.

plan.nicheHint: Compare where your visitors came from. The channel that sends the most interested {audience} deserves more of your time next month.

stageHints.idea: Low numbers are normal this early; you are building a baseline.
stageHints.started: Compare these numbers with what happened before this month's changes.
stageHints.some_traction: Look at which channel brought buyers, not just visitors.
stageHints.already_earning: Compare conversion rates across your products to see which pages need work.

plan.missionTitle: Make one change to fix your biggest bottleneck.
plan.goal: Make one focused change and note the date.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 25 lesson
tasks.description: Change one thing at a time so you can tell what worked. Learn which changes to try for traffic and for conversion.

tasks.title: Choose one change
tasks.description: For low traffic, plan more posts on your best channel. For low conversion, improve the headline, previews or FAQ.

tasks.title: Make the change
tasks.description: Do it today and keep everything else the same.

tasks.title: Log the date
tasks.description: Write the date and what you changed so you can compare numbers later.

tasks.title: Set a check-in
tasks.description: Put a reminder in one week to look at the numbers again.

plan.nicheHint: If the page is the issue, check whether a visitor from {audience} can see within seconds that it solves {problem}.

stageHints.idea: If you have very few visits, focus on traffic before changing the page.
stageHints.started: Try a clearer headline in the words your audience used.
stageHints.some_traction: Try better preview images that show the inside of the product.
stageHints.already_earning: Test one change on your best seller's page, where you get enough visits to learn.

plan.missionTitle: Plan a simple bundle or upsell for buyers who want more.
plan.goal: Write down one bundle or upsell idea with a price.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 26 lesson
tasks.description: An upsell or bundle gives buyers who want more a clear next step. Learn simple options that fit small products.

tasks.title: Look at buyer questions
tasks.description: Note what buyers asked for after using the product.

tasks.title: Pick one idea
tasks.description: Choose one: a bigger version, a companion template, a bundle of related items or a printed-ready extra.

tasks.title: Price it
tasks.description: Use the pricing worksheet to price it fairly against the main product.

tasks.title: Sketch an outline
tasks.description: Write a short outline. You do not need to build it this month.

plan.nicheHint: Think about the next problem {audience} hit after solving {problem}. That is often your best upsell or companion product.

stageHints.idea: Just write the idea down; focus on your first product for now.
stageHints.started: Plan a small add-on that fixes what testers said was missing.
stageHints.some_traction: Plan a companion product your buyers asked for and note its price.
stageHints.already_earning: Group your existing products into a bundle with a clear combined price.

plan.missionTitle: Send a helpful email to your list that mentions your product.
plan.goal: Send one helpful email.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 27 lesson
tasks.description: The best product emails teach something first. Learn a simple structure you can reuse every week.

tasks.title: Pick one tip
tasks.description: Choose one useful tip from your product or posts.

tasks.title: Write the email
tasks.description: Share the tip, a short story or example, and one line about the product.

tasks.title: Send it
tasks.description: Send it to your list, even if it is small.

tasks.title: Note the results
tasks.description: Write down opens, clicks and replies.

plan.nicheHint: Send {audience} one quick tip for {problem} they can use today, then mention how the product helps with the rest.

stageHints.idea: A short email to a handful of people still counts.
stageHints.started: Tell your list about the improved version and why you changed it.
stageHints.some_traction: Share a buyer result, with permission, as the story in your email.
stageHints.already_earning: Plan a regular email rhythm that rotates between tips and products.

plan.missionTitle: Batch your content so sharing your product does not take over your week.
plan.goal: Plan and prepare next week's content.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 28 lesson
tasks.description: A simple weekly routine keeps your product visible without burning you out. Learn how to batch.

tasks.title: Pick a rhythm
tasks.description: Choose a number of posts and one email per week you can keep up.

tasks.title: Batch next week
tasks.description: Create next week's posts in one session.

tasks.title: Reuse what worked
tasks.description: Repeat the topic or format that got the most clicks, with a new angle.

tasks.title: Schedule it
tasks.description: Use free scheduling where available, or set reminders.

plan.nicheHint: Plan four posts for {audience} that each solve a small piece of {problem}. Reuse the formats that already got clicks.

stageHints.idea: Pick a rhythm that feels almost too easy; consistency matters more.
stageHints.started: Reuse your best posts from launch week in a new format.
stageHints.some_traction: Double down on the channel that brought buyers.
stageHints.already_earning: Batch content for all your products in one weekly session.

plan.missionTitle: Deal with doubts, slow sales and tricky buyer situations.
plan.goal: Write your plan for slow weeks and refund requests.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 29 lesson
tasks.description: Slow sales, self-doubt and refund requests are normal. Learn calm, practical ways to handle each one.

tasks.title: Write your refund policy
tasks.description: Decide your policy, make sure it follows your platform's rules and add it to your page.

tasks.title: Plan for slow weeks
tasks.description: Write three things you will do in a week with no sales, such as post, email and improve the page.

tasks.title: List your wins
tasks.description: Write everything you have finished this month. Most people never publish a product.

tasks.title: Handle doubts with facts
tasks.description: When you feel like a fraud, reread the feedback and questions you collected.

plan.nicheHint: Remember that {audience} need practical help with {problem}, not perfection. Being a few steps ahead is enough to help.

stageHints.idea: Finishing and publishing is already a real result; be proud of it.
stageHints.started: Write down what you would do differently from your first attempt.
stageHints.some_traction: Note which actions led to sales so you can repeat them in slow weeks.
stageHints.already_earning: Write a plan for steady weeks and launch weeks so you do not burn out.

plan.missionTitle: Review your month and plan the next 30 days.
plan.goal: Write your next 30-day plan.

tasks.title: Watch the Day 30 lesson
tasks.description: Look back at your month with honest numbers and turn what you learned into a focused next plan.

tasks.title: Write your numbers
tasks.description: Note visits, conversion rate, sales, revenue and email subscribers.

tasks.title: Write three lessons
tasks.description: What worked, what did not and what you would change.

tasks.title: Pick one focus
tasks.description: Choose one focus for the next 30 days, such as more traffic, a better page or a second product.

tasks.title: Plan the next month
tasks.description: Write weekly goals for the next 30 days, using the launch checklist for anything new.

plan.nicheHint: Decide whether next month is about reaching more {audience}, improving how you solve {problem}, or adding a second product they asked for.

stageHints.idea: Plan to keep sharing your product for another 30 days; most products need time.
stageHints.started: Plan to focus on the bottleneck your numbers showed.
stageHints.some_traction: Plan to grow what already brings sales before adding something new.
stageHints.already_earning: Plan your next product or bundle and keep improving your best seller.

resources.title: Product Validation Worksheet
resources.description: Check that people want help with your problem before you build. Fill it in over Days 2 to 4.

sections.heading: Questions people ask
body: Write 15 questions copied word for word from Reddit, Pinterest, Etsy reviews or YouTube comments.
Note where you found each one.
Group them into three or four themes.

sections.heading: What already sells
body: List 10 similar products with format, price and rough review count.
Note what buyers praise and what they wish was included.
Write one sentence on how your version could be clearer or more specific.

sections.heading: Tiny survey
body: Ask: what do you struggle with, what have you tried, what would help most?
Share only with friends or in places where surveys are allowed.
Write the top two answers here.

sections.heading: Decision
body: Is the problem asked about often?
Do similar products already sell?
If both are yes, move on. If not, adjust the problem or audience.

resources.title: Product Outline Template
resources.description: Plan your product backwards from the result so version 1 stays small and finishable.

sections.heading: End result
body: After using this, the buyer will be able to...
They will have these files or pages...

sections.heading: Sections
body: Start here: how to use the product.
Sections 1 to 6: one step each, in order.
Wrap up: what to do next.

sections.heading: Cut list
body: Write anything that is nice to know but not needed.
Move it to a later version or a bonus.

sections.heading: What is included
body: Format: PDF, template link, printable or video.
Number of pages, files or lessons.
What is not included, stated plainly.

resources.title: Licensing and Copyright Checklist
resources.description: Make sure everything in your product is yours to sell. Go through it before publishing and whenever you add assets.

sections.heading: Your content
body: Everything is written in your own words.
You are not reselling other people's work or PLR content as your own.
Any quotes are short and credited.

sections.heading: Fonts and images
body: Each font's license allows commercial use in products for sale.
Each image is your own or licensed for use in products for sale.
Keep a note or screenshot of each license.

sections.heading: Templates and tools
body: Check the terms of any template you started from before reselling a design based on it.
Follow the rules of tools such as Canva or Notion on what can be sold.
Never include brand logos or characters you do not have rights to.

sections.heading: Sensitive topics
body: For health, finance or legal topics, frame the product as educational.
Add a clear disclaimer that it is not professional advice.
Follow your selling platform's rules for your category.

resources.title: Sales Page Template
resources.description: A simple, honest structure for your product page. Fill each part in plain words.

sections.heading: Headline and promise
body: Name the result in your audience's words.
Add one line on who it is for.
Avoid promises you cannot keep, such as guaranteed income or results.

sections.heading: Who it is for
body: This is for you if... (three bullets).
This is not for you if... (one or two bullets).

sections.heading: What is inside
body: List every file, page or lesson.
Say the format and how delivery works.
Add three preview images that show real pages.

sections.heading: Price and FAQ
body: State the price clearly.
Answer: how do I get it, what devices does it work on, what is your refund policy?
Add real testimonials once you have them, with permission.

resources.title: Pricing Worksheet
resources.description: Set a fair beginner price you can explain, then revisit it once you have real sales.

sections.heading: Market range
body: Lowest price of similar products.
Most common price.
Highest price and what makes it different.

sections.heading: Value
body: How much time or stress does it save?
How complete is it compared with others?
Is it a quick tool or a full system?

sections.heading: Your price
body: Pick one number inside the range.
Write one sentence on why it is fair.
Avoid pricing far below everyone just because you are new.

sections.heading: Review later
body: Revisit after your first sales or after a month.
Change price separately from other changes so you can tell what worked.

resources.title: Launch Checklist
resources.description: Everything to check before and after your product goes live.

sections.heading: Before publishing
body: Title names the result.
Price is set and the refund policy is written.
Files are uploaded and open correctly on phone and computer.
Preview images show real pages.

sections.heading: Page details
body: What is included is listed clearly.
FAQ answers delivery, devices and refunds.
Licensing checklist is complete.

sections.heading: Test
body: Use preview or a test purchase to confirm delivery.
Check that the email or download link arrives.

sections.heading: After publishing
body: Save your link.
Add it to your bio.
Share with ten people or one community, following its rules.

text.digital_products:
The best first product solves one specific problem your audience already asks about.

1. Write down who you want to help and five problems they have.
2. Search Reddit, Pinterest and YouTube comments for those problems and copy real questions.
3. Pick the problem that comes up most and choose a small format, such as a checklist, template or short guide.

Next step: write one sentence: I help [audience] with [problem] using a [format].

followUps: How do I check if people will buy it?
Which format is easiest to start with?
How small should my first product be?

text.digital_products:
You cannot know for sure until people buy, but you can lower the risk a lot before you build.

1. Collect 15 real questions about the problem from places your audience talks.
2. Look for similar products already selling and note their prices and reviews.
3. Ask five people who fit your audience a short three-question survey.

If people ask about it often and similar products sell, that is a good enough signal to build a small version 1.

Next step: open the Product Validation Worksheet and fill in the first section.

followUps: Where do I find real questions?
What if there is a lot of competition?
How do I write survey questions?

text.digital_products:
Start with a fair price inside the range similar products already sell for.

1. Note the prices of 10 similar products and find the most common one.
2. Think about how much time or stress your product saves and how complete it is.
3. Pick one number in the range and write one sentence on why it is fair.

Avoid pricing far below everyone just because you are new; very low prices can make a product look less useful. You can change it later, one change at a time.

Next step: fill in the Pricing Worksheet.

followUps: Should I offer a discount at launch?
When should I raise my price?
Is a free product a good idea?

text.digital_products:
No sales in the first weeks is very common, and the fix depends on your numbers.

1. Check your page visits. If very few people have seen the page, the issue is traffic, not the product.
2. If you have had a fair number of visits and no sales, look at the headline, preview images and what is included.
3. Ask a few people who fit your audience what stopped them from buying.

Change one thing at a time so you can tell what helped.

Next step: write down your visits and sales from the last two weeks.

followUps: How do I get more visitors?
How do I improve my sales page?
Should I lower my price?

text.digital_products:
There is no single best platform. Pick one that fits your product and your audience, and start.

1. Marketplaces such as Etsy have shoppers already browsing but more competition and rules.
2. Storefronts such as Gumroad, Payhip, Stan or Ko-fi give you a simple page you send people to yourself.
3. Check each one's current fees and rules for digital products before you decide.

You can add a second platform later if your buyers clearly shop there.

Next step: compare two platforms in a short table and pick one today.

followUps: What should I set up first on my platform?
Can I sell on two platforms at once?
How do platform fees work?

text.digital_products:
A clear sales page answers six questions: what it does, who it is for, what is inside, what it costs, what it looks like and what if.

1. Write the headline using your audience's own words for the problem.
2. List exactly what is included: format, pages and files.
3. Add three preview images that show real pages, and a short FAQ with your refund policy.

Keep it honest: no guaranteed results.

Next step: open the Sales Page Template and write your headline.

followUps: How do I write a better headline?
How do I make preview images?
What should go in my FAQ?

text.digital_products:
You can get your first visitors without ads by being helpful where your audience already spends time.

1. Pick one or two channels, such as Pinterest, short videos or a community you belong to.
2. Turn the questions you collected into helpful posts that each solve a small problem.
3. End each post with one link to your product or free resource.

In communities, read the rules first and only share your link where it is allowed.

Next step: write three post ideas from your question list.

followUps: What should I post about?
How often should I post?
How do I use Pinterest for products?

text.digital_products:
An email list lets you reach interested people directly, and you can start it for free.

1. Make a small free resource that solves one tiny part of the problem.
2. Set up a signup form with your selling platform's email feature or a free email tool.
3. Send a welcome email that delivers the freebie and says what to expect.

Only email people who signed up, and include an unsubscribe link.

Next step: pick one idea from the Lead Magnet Ideas guide.

followUps: What should my lead magnet be?
What do I write in a welcome email?
How often should I email?

text.digital_products:
Feeling unqualified is very common when you make your first product.

1. You do not need to be the top expert, only a few steps ahead of the people you help.
2. Reread the questions you collected; they show people need this help.
3. Be honest about what your product covers and what it does not.

For health, finance or legal topics, keep it educational and add a clear disclaimer.

Next step: write three things you know now that you wish you had known earlier.

followUps: How do I find my angle?
How do I share without feeling pushy?
What if someone criticizes my product?

text.digital_products:
Refund requests happen to every seller, and a calm, fair policy protects you and your buyers.

1. Write a clear refund policy that follows your platform's rules and put it on your page.
2. When someone asks, reply politely, ask what did not work and handle it according to your policy.
3. Use what they tell you to make the product or the page clearer.

Being clear about what is included up front prevents many refund requests.

Next step: write your refund policy in two or three sentences.

followUps: What should my refund policy say?
How do I reply to an unhappy buyer?
How do I prevent refunds?

text.digital_products:
Everything in your product should be yours or properly licensed for use in products you sell.

1. Write the content in your own words. Do not resell PLR or other people's material as your own.
2. Use fonts and images whose license allows commercial use in products for sale, and keep notes.
3. Check the terms of any tool or template you used before selling designs made with it.

If you are unsure about a specific case, check the license directly or ask a qualified professional.

Next step: go through the Licensing and Copyright Checklist.

followUps: Can I use Canva elements in products I sell?
What is PLR?
Do I need a disclaimer?

text.digital_products:
A bundle or upsell gives buyers who want more a clear next step.

1. Look at what buyers ask for after using your first product.
2. Pick one idea: a companion template, a bigger version or a bundle of related items.
3. Price it fairly against your main product using the Pricing Worksheet.

Focus on getting your first product seen before building many more.

Next step: write one upsell idea and a rough outline.

followUps: How should I price a bundle?
When should I make a second product?
What makes a good companion product?

text.digital_products:
Most first products stall because they are too big or aiming for perfect.

1. Cut your outline to the sections that are needed for the result.
2. Work in short, fixed sessions and write [fix later] when you get stuck.
3. Remember you can update the file after launch and send buyers the new version.

A finished small product teaches you more than a perfect unfinished one.

Next step: pick the next section and work on it for 30 minutes.

followUps: How small should version 1 be?
How do I make time for this?
How do I update my product after launch?

text.digital_products:
Good question. Tell me a bit more so I can be specific: who your product is for, what stage it is at and what you are trying to improve.

Until then, the rule that fixes most early product problems is simple: finish the next small step and put it in front of real people. One published page teaches more than a week of planning.

Next step: open Today's Mission and finish the first task, then come back with details.

followUps: What should I do today?
What product should I make?
How do I get my first sale?
